verdict_reasoning: No surviving objection questions the goal, and a committer who knows this code supports it in message #3. Three fixable design points remain: the hot standby argument for 0003 (replication-ondisk-1), the undocumented pairing of a plain atomic write with the barrier in LWLockRelease (maintenance-fit-1), and the missing benchmarks (maintenance-fit-2). None of them stops review; each needs sign-off from someone who knows procarray.c.

brief.title: Lockless snapshot reuse in GetSnapshotData
brief.problem: GetSnapshotData() takes ProcArrayLock in shared mode even when it only checks that a cached snapshot is still valid. That shared acquisition writes to the lock's cache line, which costs time on busy systems with many backends. The author's test-suite count shows about half of calls could skip the lock.
brief.proposed_design: An atomic read of TransamVariables->xactCompletionCount replaces the locked check when a backend reuses its cached snapshot. 0002 does this only when MyProc->xmin is already set. 0003 also installs the snapshot's xmin without the lock, then reads the counter again and falls back to the locked path if it changed. 0001 moves TransamVariablesData into a new varsup.h so it can hold atomic types.
user_visible_surface: New header src/include/access/varsup.h holds TransamVariablesData, and extensions that use TransamVariables must include it.
TransamVariables->xactCompletionCount becomes an atomic type, so C code that reads it must change.
author_claims: About 50% of GetSnapshotData() calls in the regression suite take the lockless path in v1, and 37% miss it only because no xmin is set.
The change saves write traffic on the ProcArrayLock cache line in some workloads.
Setting xmin without an exclusive lock is safe, because only the owning backend writes its xmin, already under LW_SHARED today.
With 0003, vacuum horizons can move backward in more cases, and the author treats this as acceptable because other code already does it.
Commit 623a9ba79b already pointed to this optimization.
brief.thread_state: Andres Freund and Bertrand Drouvot support the idea and accept the xmin reasoning behind 0003. Open points: documenting the pairing of a plain atomic write with a membarrier read, a cheaper first read, and benchmarks.
unclear: No benchmark shows throughput or latency gains; the only numbers are call counts from the regression suite.
The thread does not show how often backward vacuum horizons happen with 0003, or what harm they could cause.
The patch does not say if moving only xactCompletionCount out of TransamVariables was tried, or what that costs writers.
The thread does not show the extra cost of the membarrier reads on weakly ordered platforms such as ARM.
The thread does not say how hot standby and the KnownAssignedXids path are affected.

prior_attempts.title: POC: Cache data in GetSnapshotData()
prior_attempts.quote: As Andres has suggested previously I need a mechanism to identify and avoid caching for such scenarios.
prior_attempts.reason: No closing message is shown. In 2016 Robert Haas returned the patch until the CLOG contention work was settled. At the 2017 decision three issues were open: the read-only gain appeared only on machines with more than two sockets, Robert Haas called the small regression at 1 client concerning, and the author had no way yet to skip caching when quick write transactions invalidate the cache before it is reused.
prior_attempts.what_is_different: P3 shared one snapshot across backends in shared memory and paid for the cache when writes invalidated it. This proposal keeps the existing per-backend cache and only drops the lock from the validity check, with a fallback to the locked path.

prior_attempts.title: Move PinBuffer and UnpinBuffer to atomics
prior_attempts.quote: Which you made ineffective because PinBuffer() doesn't take a lock anymore. Mutual exclusion through locks only works if all participants take the locks.
prior_attempts.reason: Andres Freund judged the first patch incorrect. PinBuffer no longer took the header lock, but StrategyGetBuffer, SyncOneBuffer and BufferAlloc still relied on that lock for mutual exclusion. Work moved to the single atomic state version, which Alexander Korotkov refactored and others benchmarked, and it was still being cleaned up when the entry closed. No visible message states why the entry was returned.
prior_attempts.what_is_different: P2 removed a lock that other code still relied on for mutual exclusion. Here only the owning backend writes its xmin, and a second read of the counter replaces the exclusion against committers.

prior_attempts.title: Revert changes to CONCURRENTLY that "sped up" Xmin advance
prior_attempts.quote: In other words, Xmin advancement was sped up, but at the cost of corrupting the resulting index.
prior_attempts.reason:
This reverts commit d9d076222f5b "VACUUM: ignore indexing operations
with CONCURRENTLY".

These changes caused indexes created with the CONCURRENTLY option to
miss heap tuples that were HOT-updated and HOT-pruned during the index
creation.  Before these changes, HOT pruning would have been prevented
by the Xmin of the transaction creating the index, but because this
change was precisely to allow the Xmin to move forward ignoring that
backend, now other backends scanning the table can prune them.  This is
not a problem for VACUUM (which requires a lock that conflicts with a
CREATE INDEX CONCURRENTLY operation), but HOT-prune can definitely
occur.  In other words, Xmin advancement was sped up, but at the cost of
corrupting the resulting index.

Regrettably, this means that the new feature in PG14 that RIC/CIC on
very large tables no longer force VACUUM to retain very old tuples goes
away.  We might try to implement it again in a later release, but for
now the risk of indexes missing tuples is too high and there's no easy
fix.

Backpatch to 14, where this change appeared.

prior_attempts.what_is_different: P11 let horizons ignore a backend's xmin. 0003 installs the xmin without the lock and rechecks the counter, which is a different mechanism.

objections.title: Lockless xmin install in 0003 has no stated argument for hot standby
objections.failure_scenario: On a hot standby, a backend with a cached snapshot and no xmin installs that snapshot's old xmin without ProcArrayLock while the startup process replays a prune record. The startup process checks for conflicts, sees no xmin on that backend, and removes the tuples. The backend's counter check passes because no completion was replayed, so the query reads pages missing rows it should see.
objections.argument: The safety argument in message #5 covers only primary-side writers: owner-only writes to xmin, plus transaction completion bumping xactCompletionCount. On a standby, other events advance horizons: prune replay with recovery conflicts, and KnownAssignedXids expiry from running-xacts records for xids that never got an abort record. The lockless path is safe only if every such event either bumps xactCompletionCount or cannot pass an xmin that a valid reused snapshot still needs. Message #6 accepts the reasoning without discussing standby, and the patch adds no rule that future standby code must follow.
objections.author_must_show: On a hot standby, which replay events can remove data a reused snapshot needs without bumping xactCompletionCount, and why does 0003 still never return wrong results?

precedents.title: Revert changes to CONCURRENTLY that "sped up" Xmin advance

critic.reasoning: The thread gives no argument for hot standby, so the request stands. The scenario is weaker than stated, because the conflict check and GetSnapshotData both take ProcArrayLock in shared mode today, and [P11] concerns a different mechanism and must not be used as support.

objections.title: Counter correctness depends on an undocumented barrier in LWLockRelease
objections.failure_scenario: A later patch moves an xactCompletionCount increment outside the ProcArrayLock exclusive section, for example into group clear or a new completion path, or changes LWLockRelease ordering. The lockless reader can then see a stale count and reuse a snapshot that misses a commit. No test fails; users see wrong visibility results long after release.
objections.argument: Message #6 notes that IncrementXactCompletionCount() uses a plain pg_atomic_write_u64() and relies on the full barrier in the following LWLockRelease(ProcArrayLock), and that no other code in the tree uses this pairing. Message #3 asks for the same pairing to be documented. Today the Assert on LW_EXCLUSIVE guards the lock, but nothing ties the read side's correctness to that release barrier. Each future completion path must preserve an invariant that is visible only in comments.
objections.author_must_show: What fails loudly, by assertion or by API shape, if a future increment site stops being followed by a barrier-carrying release?

precedents.title: Move PinBuffer and UnpinBuffer to atomics

critic.reasoning: Message #6 asks for the pairing of the plain write with the barrier in LWLockRelease to be documented, and the thread has no answer yet. The assert on LW_EXCLUSIVE covers part of the scenario, and [P2] is about a different error and adds no support.

objections.title: No measurement of the new path, including membarrier reads on ARM
objections.failure_scenario: On a weakly ordered platform, every snapshot taken by every backend now does one or two pg_atomic_read_membarrier_u64() calls. A workload with frequent commits fails the counter check and takes the lock anyway, so it pays for both. An OLTP user on ARM finds a regression only after upgrading.
objections.argument: The only numbers are call counts from the regression suite (message #1); in message #5 the author asserts that membarrier reads cost less than the lock acquisition but shows no measurement. Messages #2 and #6 ask for benchmarks, and message #6 proposes a cheaper first read. GetSnapshotData() is on the path of nearly every query, so the cost falls on all users. In [P3], snapshot reuse work stalled on a regression at low client counts and on workloads where commits invalidate the cache before it is reused.
objections.author_must_show: What throughput do x86 and ARM show at 1 client and at high client counts, for read-only and commit-heavy pgbench runs?

critic.reasoning: The thread shows only call counts, and messages #2 and #6 ask for benchmarks that no later message provides. [P3] cached snapshots in shared memory, a different design, so it must not be used as support.

refuted.title: 0003 installs xmin locklessly without a stated horizon invariant
refuted.failure_scenario: Backend A installs a reused snapshot's xmin without ProcArrayLock while backend B computes GlobalVis horizons and HOT-prunes a page. If B's horizon ever passes A's new xmin, B removes tuple versions A's snapshot still needs. A returns wrong rows, and users find out only through inconsistent query results or a corrupt index.
refuted.argument: Message #3 reports that the original xactCompletionCount work dropped this lockless path because of "nagging doubts that it was entirely safe". 0003 now goes further and drops the lock for xmin installation too. Message #5 says this makes retreating vacuum horizons more common and accepts that by analogy to existing code; messages #5 and #6 argue the double counter check, but neither says which pruning or horizon consumer is shown safe against a retreating horizon. [P11] records a horizon shortcut that looked benign and was reverted because HOT pruning removed tuples an index build still needed.
refuted.author_must_show: Which invariant guarantees that no backend can compute a pruning horizon above the xmin 0003 installs, including GlobalVis caches and hot standby?

precedents.title: Revert changes to CONCURRENTLY that "sped up" Xmin advance

critic.reasoning: Messages #5 and #6 state the rule for the primary: an unchanged counter means every xid the snapshot saw as running still runs, and the second read catches a completion. The hot standby part is a duplicate of replication-ondisk-1, and [P11] removed a backend from horizons, a different mechanism.

refuted.title: Moving all of TransamVariablesData forces extension changes for one counter
refuted.failure_scenario: An out-of-tree extension that reads TransamVariables, for example for nextXid or oldestXid, stops compiling against the new major version until it includes varsup.h. C code that reads xactCompletionCount must also switch to atomic accessors. Extension maintainers find out at their next build.
refuted.argument: 0001 touches 16 files to move the whole struct, because only xactCompletionCount needs an atomic type. Message #2 suggests moving only that counter and notes the cost of a second cache line for writers; the material does not show that comparison. The narrower move would leave the extension-facing header unchanged. Message #3 asked only for 0001 to be a separate commit, so the scope question is still open.
refuted.author_must_show: What does moving only xactCompletionCount cost committing backends, measured, compared with splitting the whole TransamVariablesData into varsup.h?

critic.reasoning: An extension that must add one include on a new major version is routine and is not a failure. Message #2 says only procarray.c uses xactCompletionCount, and the cache-line cost of the narrower move belongs to the benchmark request in maintenance-fit-2.

refuted.title: Gain is shown only as call counts, not as throughput
refuted.failure_scenario: The series is committed. Extensions that read TransamVariables must now include varsup.h and handle an atomic xactCompletionCount. On write-heavy workloads most reuse attempts still fall back to the lock, after extra membarrier reads, and no benchmark exists to show whether anyone gained.
refuted.argument: The only numbers are regression-suite call counts (message #1), and that suite is not a production workload. Message #3 reports wins in a bunch of workloads but gives no numbers. Messages #2 and #6 ask for benchmarks of the membarrier reads, and the thread does not answer them. The cost to extension code and to weakly ordered platforms is concrete, so the gain should be measured too.
refuted.author_must_show: Which pgbench or similar workloads, at what client counts and on which hardware, gain throughput from 0002 and 0003, and do write-heavy or ARM workloads get slower?

critic.reasoning: Duplicate of maintenance-fit-2, which asks for the same benchmarks. As a desirability objection it is weak, because in message #3 a committer who knows this code says the change is a win in several workloads and should be done.

committability.owner_note: Andres Freund, who worked on the original xactCompletionCount code, reviews the patch in message #3 and says the optimization ought to be done.
committability.liability: The owner signs for snapshot correctness on primary and hot standby under a lockless protocol, with no time limit. Errors would show as wrong query results or missing tuples, and no test is likely to catch them.
committability.author_follow_up: The author posted a v2 series in message #5 that splits the header move into its own commit, as message #3 asked.

priority.reason: The gain goes to busy systems with many backends, and a committer who knows the area is engaged. The patches are small, but lockless reasoning in procarray.c needs careful review, and the memory-ordering rule must be kept by all later completion paths.

provisional_note: The code was not read, so the barrier placement, the order of the xmin write and the second counter read, and the hot standby paths could not be checked. The safety of 0003 rests on arguments in messages #5 and #6 that this review saw only through the brief and the objections.

precedents_retrieved.title: Atomic pgrename on Windows
precedents_retrieved.objectors: Andres Freund, Magnus Hagander, David Steele
precedents_retrieved.summary: The patch made pgrename() on Windows replace the target file atomically, even when another process has it open, by calling ReplaceFile() when the target exists and MoveFileEx() otherwise. It aimed to fix "Permission denied" errors seen when renaming the statistics temp file on loaded Windows servers.
precedents_retrieved.objection: Reviewers questioned the approach. Andres Freund asked why opening files with FILE_SHARE_DELETE does not already prevent the error, and suggested retry logic instead. Magnus Hagander proposed trying MoveFileEx() first and falling back to ReplaceFile() on a sharing violation, possibly with a retry loop. The commitfest manager marked it Returned with Feedback because a new patch was needed, and the author agreed both approaches still had to be implemented and tested.
precedents_retrieved.key_quote: Even so, it looks like the approach needs a rethink so better to wait for that.

precedents_retrieved.title: Fix typo 586/686 in atomics/arch-x86.h
precedents_retrieved.summary: The patch fixes misspelled macros in src/include/port/atomics/arch-x86.h, where `__i568__` and `__i668__` should be `__i586__` and `__i686__`. These checks select the x86 code paths for 8-byte atomic operations on 32-bit gcc builds.
precedents_retrieved.objection: Reviewers suggested removing the broken checks rather than fixing them, since no one had complained since 2017. Andres Freund is quoted saying the 32-bit special handling should be dropped instead of fixing the typos, and the author then returned the patch himself. His follow-up idea to drop 32-bit support entirely was opposed by Tom Lane, Nathan Bossart and Andres Freund.
precedents_retrieved.key_quote: That indeed looks like a clear typo, but if noone has complained since 2017 then maybe removing the checks is the right course of action?

precedents_retrieved.title: Atomic rename feature for Windows
precedents_retrieved.summary: The patch makes pgrename() on Windows use SetFileInformationByHandle with FILE_RENAME_FLAG_POSIX_SEMANTICS, so a rename can replace a file that is still open, as on POSIX. It raised _WIN32_WINNT to Windows 10 and added a manifest so IsWindows10OrGreater() works; a later version used the feature only on Windows build 17763 and up.
precedents_retrieved.objection: The entry closed because Thomas Munro rebased and simplified the patch and moved the work to a new thread and CommitFest entry. the entry for this thread [2].

precedents_retrieved.title: Revert GetTransactionSnapshot() to return historic snapshot during LR
precedents_retrieved.summary:
Revert GetTransactionSnapshot() to return historic snapshot during LR
Reverted commit(s): Don't allow GetTransactionSnapshot() in logical decoding
precedents_retrieved.objection:
Commit 1585ff7387 changed GetTransactionSnapshot() to throw an error
if it's called during logical decoding, instead of returning the
historic snapshot. I made that change for extra protection, because a
historic snapshot can only be used to access catalog tables while
GetTransactionSnapshot() is usually called when you're executing
arbitrary queries. You might get very subtle visibility problems if
you tried to use the historic snapshot for arbitrary queries.

There's no built-in code in PostgreSQL that calls
GetTransactionSnapshot() during logical decoding, but it turns out
that the pglogical extension does just that, to evaluate row filter
expressions. You would get weird results if the row filter runs
arbitrary queries, but it is sane as long as you don't access any
non-catalog tables. Even though there are no checks to enforce that in
pglogical, a typical row filter expression does not access any tables
and works fine. Accessing tables marked with the user_catalog_table =
true option is also OK.

To fix pglogical with row filters, and any other extensions that might
do similar things, revert GetTransactionSnapshot() to return a
historic snapshot during logical decoding.

To try to still catch the unsafe usage of historic snapshots, add
checks in heap_beginscan() and index_beginscan() to complain if you
try to use a historic snapshot to scan a non-catalog table. We're very
close to the version 18 release however, so add those new checks only
in master.

roaster_notes.note: 0002 (lockless reuse with xmin already set) has no prior rejection whose reason still applies, and P16 has no recorded reason, so it is not used.

The proposal adds no SQL syntax, GUC, catalog object, psql feature or dump content, and existing queries return the same results. The only user-facing change is the new varsup.h header, which extensions that use TransamVariables must include. That kind of header reorganization is routine in a major release and easy to adapt to. Vacuum horizon retreat and memory ordering are safety questions outside this angle.

The proposal adds no on-disk format, WAL record, catalog or wire-protocol change. The header split and atomic type change in 0001 and 0002 touch extension source code only on master, which is routine across major versions. The one open point from this angle is hot standby correctness for 0003. P11 is cited only as an example of an xmin-advance change that was safe for vacuum but not for HOT pruning.

The proposal changes how a backend checks its own cached snapshot inside procarray.c. It adds no SQL surface, privilege, setting, view or log output, and no user can reach or observe the new path in a new way. Correctness of the lockless xmin publication and of backward vacuum horizons is a data-safety question for the design angle, not a privilege or exposure issue.
No fit objection: the change is core procarray work, and Andres Freund, who wrote the original snapshot scalability code, supports it (message #3).

This is an internal locking change in GetSnapshotData(), so no setting, extension or hook could give the same result. It extends the existing xactCompletionCount reuse mechanism instead of adding a second one, so this angle has no objection.

Demand for the goal is credible: it affects every backend that takes snapshots, Andres Freund planned it in 623a9ba79b, and two reviewers support it. The one open point is the size of the gain, which is not yet measured.
